# Scattering orders and the spatial inversion {#sec-scattering-orders}

## The physical question {#sec-scattering-orders-question}

@sec-angular-system solves a tridiagonal system and returns angular
coefficients $h_\ell(k,\omega)$. Two things stand between that and a response
at a point.

The first is that the answer should not be one opaque number. Light that
reaches the module without scattering, light that scattered exactly once, and
light that scattered twice or more behave differently in time, are singular in
different ways, and are accurate for different reasons. Separating them is not
cosmetic: two of the three are computed by routes that do not go through
@eq-angular-system at all, because those routes are better.

The second is that $h_\ell(k,\omega)$ lives in wavenumber space. Getting back
to a displacement $\mathbf r$ means an inverse Fourier transform, and in a
medium whose response depends only on $r=\lvert\mathbf r\rvert$ and on the
angle to the source axis that transform collapses onto one radial integral per
angular degree, against a spherical Bessel function. That integral is where the
finiteness of the calculation finally bites: it runs over $0\le k<\infty$ and
the code evaluates it on a finite grid.

Four quantities are easy to conflate and are independent throughout this
chapter. The **number of collisions** is a physical index, $0$, $1$, $\ge2$.
The **scattering degree** $L$ truncates the angular rank of the medium
operator, @eq-gamma. The **spatial degree** $J$ is how many angular
coefficients the inversion keeps. The **wavenumber range** $k_{\max}$ and its
quadrature are a separate numerical approximation again. A statement about one
is not a statement about another.

## Assumptions and definitions {#sec-scattering-orders-assumptions}

One wavelength; the medium homogeneous, unbounded and reciprocal; $\mu_a>0$.
The geometry of this chapter is a **point** source and a **point** isotropic
receiver, so the angular problem is the $m=0$ problem of
@sec-angular-system-m-zero. Displacement $\mathbf r$ points from the emission
point to the observation point, $r=\lvert\mathbf r\rvert$, and for a directed
source of emission direction $\hat{\mathbf s}_0$,
$$
\nu=\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}_0 .
$$ {#eq-orders-nu}

Write $G_0=D^{-1}$ for the **free resolvent** — multiplication by
$1/(d_0+ik\mu)$, the operator that propagates without scattering — and
$\Gamma$ for the scattering operator, diagonal in the basis of
@sec-angular-system-basis with entries $\gamma_\ell$ from @eq-gamma. The
response per unit effective area at the observation point is written
$$
K=K^{(0)}+K^{(1)}+K^{(\ge2)},
$$ {#eq-orders-split}
with units $\mathrm m^{-2}$ per unit frequency content, the units of
`GreenResult`.

## Derivation {#sec-scattering-orders-derivation}

### Splitting the solve by collisions {#sec-scattering-orders-split}

@eq-angular-starting-point is $(D-\Gamma)h=1$ in this notation. Expanding the
resolvent,
$$
h=(D-\Gamma)^{-1}\mathbf 1
=G_0\mathbf 1+G_0\Gamma G_0\mathbf 1+G_0\Gamma G_0\Gamma G_0\mathbf 1+\cdots,
$$
each term carrying one more factor of $\Gamma$, that is one more collision.
Grouping the first two terms and everything else:
$$
h^{(0)}=G_0\mathbf 1,
$$ {#eq-order-zero}
$$
h^{(1)}=G_0\,\Gamma\,h^{(0)},
$$ {#eq-order-one}
$$
h^{(\ge2)}=(D-\Gamma)^{-1}\,\Gamma\,h^{(1)} .
$$ {#eq-order-two-plus}

@eq-order-two-plus deserves a sentence, because it looks like a single
scattering event and is not. The operator in front is the **full** resolvent,
not the free one, so expanding it gives
$$
(D-\Gamma)^{-1}\Gamma h^{(1)}
=\bigl(G_0+G_0\Gamma G_0+G_0\Gamma G_0\Gamma G_0+\cdots\bigr)\Gamma h^{(1)},
$$
whose terms carry two, three, four collisions and so on without limit. One
solve of the same tridiagonal system sums every order from the second upwards.
The identity that makes @eq-order-zero, @eq-order-one and @eq-order-two-plus add up to $h$ is
the resolvent identity $M^{-1}=M_0^{-1}+M^{-1}\Gamma M_0^{-1}$ with
$M=M_0-\Gamma$, applied once.

What matters numerically is what the third piece is **not**. It is not the
total minus the first two. A difference of nearly equal numbers loses the
digits that distinguish them, and at large $L$ or small scattering the
multiply-scattered part is precisely the small difference of two larger
quantities. @eq-order-two-plus computes it from its own right-hand side
$\Gamma h^{(1)}$, so its accuracy is set by its own size and not by the size of
what it was subtracted from.

In the code these three are the three arrays returned by
`lighthit.angular.angular_components`: `b` is @eq-order-zero, `first_low` is
@eq-order-one — exactly one scattering **in the finite-rank model** of degree
$L$ — and `multiple_low` is @eq-order-two-plus, the sum of all orders from two
upwards in that same model. Both of the latter are obtained by
`solve_tail_system` with the exact free tail of @eq-tail-correction: the
elimination is a property of the matrix and applies whatever the right-hand
side is.

### What the production solver actually composes {#sec-scattering-orders-production}

`PointGreenSolver` does **not** use all three. It composes
$$
K=\underbrace{K^{(0)}_{\text{analytic}}}_{\text{closed form}}
+\underbrace{K^{(1)}_{\text{full HG}}}_{\text{coordinate quadrature}}
+\underbrace{K^{(\ge2)}_{L}}_{\text{finite-rank, spatially inverted}} ,
$$ {#eq-production-composition}
and each term is computed by a different route for a reason.

The ballistic term has a closed form (@sec-scattering-orders-ballistic) and
needs no numerics at all. The first order is computed in coordinate space by
`lighthit.single`, with the **full** Henyey--Greenstein phase function and no
Legendre truncation. Two reasons, and the second is the stronger one. At first
order the integral is low-dimensional enough to do directly, and the forward
peak that $L$ struggles with is exactly where first-order light comes from. And
for a *directed* point source read by a point receiver, the first-order
response carries an integrable $1/\rho$ singularity at the ballistic root; a
singular function of $\mathbf r$ has a wavenumber content that falls off
slowly, so the multipole route of @sec-scattering-orders-inversion does not
converge for it at any practical $L$, $J$ and $k_{\max}$.
@sec-scattering-orders-example measures both statements.

Only the multiply-scattered part is taken from the angular system and inverted
in space, and it is the part for which the finite-rank model is least
demanding, because multiple scattering has already smoothed the angular
distribution.

The consequence is worth stating plainly, because it is easy to assume
otherwise: **the production point solver never spatially inverts the finite-$L$
first order**. It computes `multiple` from `angular_components` and discards
`b` and `first_low`, replacing the latter with `single_spectrum`.

The cache route is not identical, and the difference matters for later
chapters. `ResponseCache` stores two order axes, named in `MOMENT_ORDERS`:
`one_finite_L` and `two_or_more`. The ballistic term is **not** stored, because
it is a closed form that costs nothing to evaluate and a delta in time that a
smooth radial table would misrepresent. For a directed flash read by an
isotropic receiver, `directed_spectrum` replaces the stored first order by the
exact full-HG quadrature, reproducing @eq-production-composition. For an
isotropic flash read by a detector with acceptance coefficients,
`acceptance_spectrum` uses the stored `one_finite_L` by default; it will
substitute the exact quadrature only when asked with `exact_first_order` **and
only for an isotropic acceptance**, and it raises otherwise. The reason is
structural rather than incidental: `single_spectrum` returns one scalar
function of $(r,\nu)$, and folding an arbitrary directional acceptance into the
first order needs the angular distribution of arrival directions, not a single
number. Replacing the first order exactly for a general directional module is
therefore not available, and @sec-directional-om computes it from the angular
route instead.

### The ballistic term {#sec-scattering-orders-ballistic}

For an isotropic instantaneous flash of one photon, the unscattered light at
distance $r$ is the inverse-square law times the survival probability, arriving
at one instant:
$$
K^{(0)}(r,t)=\frac{e^{-\mu_t r}}{4\pi r^2}\,\delta\!\left(t-\frac{r}{v}\right),
\qquad
\tilde K^{(0)}(r,\omega)=\frac{e^{-\mu_t r}}{4\pi r^2}\,e^{i\omega r/v}.
$$ {#eq-ballistic}
The extinction $\mu_t$, not $\mu_a$, appears: a scattered photon has left this
term, whether or not it survives. The phase is $e^{+i\omega r/v}$ by
@eq-transform-forward — the transform of a delta at $t=r/v$ — and it is the
same sign as the emission-time phase of @eq-shift-theorem.

For a **directed** delta flash the situation is different and the code is
explicit about it. Off the forward ray no straight line carries light from the
source to the receiver, so $K^{(0)}=0$. Exactly on the forward ray, a point
source and a point receiver give a distribution and not a function, and
`PointGreenSolver.solve` refuses that geometry rather than returning a large
number; it also warns when the cosine approaches one, where the angular and
radial resolutions must be refined independently. A finite aperture removes the
singularity, and that is not this chapter.

### The spatial inversion {#sec-scattering-orders-inversion}

The response at displacement $\mathbf r$ is the inverse transform
@eq-transform-inverse of the solution in wavenumber space,
$$
K(\mathbf r,\omega)=\int\frac{\mathrm d^3k}{(2\pi)^3}\,
e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}\;h(\mathbf k,\omega),
$$
where $h$ depends on the direction of $\mathbf k$ only through
$\mu=\hat{\mathbf k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}_0$ and is expanded as
$h=\sum_\ell h_\ell\,p_\ell(\mu)$. Insert the plane-wave expansion
$$
e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}
=\sum_{\lambda}i^{\lambda}(2\lambda+1)\,j_\lambda(kr)\,
P_\lambda(\hat{\mathbf k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}),
$$ {#eq-plane-wave}
and do the angular integral over $\hat{\mathbf k}$ with the addition theorem,
$$
\int\mathrm d\Omega_k\,P_\lambda(\hat{\mathbf k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})\,
P_\ell(\hat{\mathbf k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}_0)
=\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}\,\delta_{\lambda\ell}\,P_\ell(\nu).
$$
The factors $4\pi/(2\pi)^3=1/2\pi^2$ collect, and what is left is one radial
integral per degree:
$$
M_\ell(r,\omega)=i^{\ell}\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{2}}
\int_0^{\infty}\frac{k^2\,\mathrm dk}{2\pi^2}\,j_\ell(kr)\,h_\ell(k,\omega),
$$ {#eq-multipole}
$$
K(r,\nu,\omega)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{J}M_\ell(r,\omega)\,P_\ell(\nu).
$$ {#eq-multipole-sum}

The division of labour is clean. $j_\ell(kr)$ performs the radial inversion:
it is what turns a wavenumber into a distance. $P_\ell(\nu)$ restores the
angular dependence on the emission direction, and it is evaluated after the
integral, which is why one table of $M_\ell$ serves every $\nu$.

How large $J$ must be depends on what angular structure has to be resolved. For
an isotropic flash read by an isotropic receiver there is no $\nu$ dependence
at all and $J=0$ suffices. For a directed source the answer varies with $\nu$,
and the number of degrees needed grows with how sharply it varies — in practice
with $k_{\max}r$, since $j_\ell(kr)$ is negligible until $\ell\lesssim kr$. No
formula for choosing $J$ is offered here, because none has been established by
measurement; @sec-validation treats it as one line of the error budget.

### The wavenumber quadrature {#sec-scattering-orders-quadrature}

@eq-multipole runs to infinity and the code does not. `SolverSettings.quadrature`
builds the rule that replaces it: a finite cutoff $k_{\max}$; the interval
$[0,k_{\max}]$ divided into panels of width $k_{\rm panel}$; a Gauss--Legendre
rule of order $k_{\rm order}$ inside each panel; and, optionally, a smooth
taper that takes the weights to zero at the top of the range instead of cutting
them off abruptly.

This is a numerical approximation, and it is a different one from everything in
@sec-angular-system. The free angular tail there is eliminated exactly; that
exactness says nothing about @eq-multipole, whose truncation at $k_{\max}$
discards real content. Six error sources are present in the route so far and
they are independent of each other:

| Source | Controlled by |
|:--|:--|
| Angular rank of the medium | $L$ |
| Retained angular degrees of the output | $J$ |
| Truncation of the radial integral | $k_{\max}$ |
| Resolution of the oscillations of $j_\ell(kr)$ | panel width |
| Accuracy inside a panel | quadrature order |
| Smoothing at the cutoff | taper |

A convergence study over all six belongs to @sec-validation. What this chapter
establishes is that they are six knobs and not one.

### The radial cache {#sec-scattering-orders-cache}

@eq-multipole depends on the medium, on $\omega$ and on $r$ — and on nothing
about the event. That is what makes a table worth building. `CacheGrid` fixes
the radii and frequencies, and `ResponseCache.build` evaluates @eq-multipole on
that grid; `ResponseCache.moments_at` interpolates between nodes. The stored
object is $M_\ell(r,\omega)$, **not** a finished answer for a particular module:
the contraction @eq-multipole-sum with $P_\ell(\nu)$, or with a detector's
acceptance coefficients, happens at query time.

Four properties of the table are mathematical rather than operational.

The radii are **geometric**, not uniform, because the response varies on a
relative scale: near and far are separated by orders of magnitude in amplitude
and by a fixed factor in every derivative that matters.

The interpolation is **cubic in $\log r$**, and before it runs the moments are
divided by a smooth positive reference,
$$
\text{scale}(r)=\frac{e^{-\mu_a r}}{4\pi r^{2}},
$$ {#eq-cache-scale}
which is restored afterwards. @eq-cache-scale removes most of the dynamic
range, so the spline interpolates a function of order unity instead of one that
falls by many decades across the table. Note the **absorption** coefficient in
@eq-cache-scale, not the extinction: the scattered orders do not decay at
$e^{-\mu_t r}$, because scattering removes light from a direction without
removing it from the medium.

With `radial_phase="flight"` the rapidly rotating factor $e^{i\omega r/v}$ is
also removed before interpolation and restored after it. That phase is the
arrival-time carrier; interpolating through it would force the spline to
resolve an oscillation in $r$ whose period shrinks as $\omega$ grows, and
removing it leaves a slowly varying envelope.

**Extrapolation is refused.** A query outside the cached radius range raises,
naming the range. A cubic spline extrapolates confidently and wrongly, and a
table that silently did so would turn an out-of-range geometry into a plausible
number.

The memory layout, the blocking of the Bessel table, the compiled backends and
the cost of a build are @sec-cache-and-memory. Nothing in this section is about
performance.

## The discrete algorithm {#sec-scattering-orders-algorithm}

1. **Build the wavenumber rule** from $k_{\max}$, the panel width, the
   quadrature order and the taper.
2. **Solve the angular system** at every wavenumber for this frequency,
   obtaining the three pieces of @eq-order-zero, @eq-order-one and @eq-order-two-plus.
3. **Tabulate** $j_\ell(kr)$ for the degrees $\ell\le J$ and the radii wanted,
   with the factor $i^\ell\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/2}\;k^2w_k/2\pi^2$ of
   @eq-multipole folded in.
4. **Contract** over wavenumbers to obtain $M_\ell(r,\omega)$, once per stored
   order.
5. **Store or contract.** Either keep $M_\ell$ on a radial grid, or contract
   immediately with $P_\ell(\nu)$ for the geometry at hand.
6. **Replace the first order** with the coordinate-space full-HG quadrature
   where the geometry allows it.
7. **Add the ballistic term** from @eq-ballistic, for an isotropic flash, or
   leave it at zero off the forward ray of a directed one.
8. **Keep the three orders separate** in the returned object, in the order
   `ballistic`, `one_exact_HG`, `two_or_more_HG_L`.

The inverse transform from $\omega$ back to time bins is @sec-time-and-bins and
is not part of this list.

## Correspondence with the code {#sec-scattering-orders-code}

| Mathematics | Symbol |
|:--|:--|
| @eq-order-zero, @eq-order-one, @eq-order-two-plus | `lighthit.angular.angular_components` |
| The wavenumber rule of @sec-scattering-orders-quadrature | `lighthit.green.SolverSettings.quadrature` |
| @eq-production-composition | `lighthit.green.PointGreenSolver.solve` |
| The three orders, kept separate | `lighthit.green.GreenResult.components` |
| First order in physical time, full HG | `lighthit.single.single_scattering_rate` |
| First order as a spectrum, full HG | `lighthit.single.single_spectrum` |
| The radial and frequency grid | `lighthit.cache.CacheGrid` |
| @eq-multipole on that grid | `lighthit.cache.ResponseCache.build` |
| Interpolated lookup, @eq-cache-scale | `lighthit.cache.ResponseCache.moments_at` |
| Directed flash, isotropic receiver | `lighthit.cache.ResponseCache.directed_spectrum` |
| Isotropic flash, detector acceptance | `lighthit.cache.ResponseCache.acceptance_spectrum` |
| The two first-order routes compared | `lighthit.cache.first_order_consistency` |

The stored order names are `lighthit.cache.MOMENT_ORDERS`, and the component
names of a saved `GreenResult` are `ballistic`, `one_exact_HG`,
`two_or_more_HG_L`. Both are part of the contract and are checked in
@sec-scattering-orders-checks.

## A worked number {#sec-scattering-orders-example}

Public synthetic medium only; the inversion is rebuilt from @eq-multipole in
the example rather than taken from the package, and the first order is checked
against a direct integration in physical time.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
NUMBA_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  python scripts/run_scattering_orders_example.py --output .build/scattering-orders-example
```

The stored output is `docs/scattering-orders-example/summary.json`, with the
configuration, the library versions, the thread settings and the exact value of
every residual quoted below as a bound.

**Configuration.** $\mu_a=0.04$, $\mu_s=0.05\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, $g=0.7$,
$n_g=1.35$; $L=8$, $J=12$, $k_{\max}=3\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ with panels of
$0.05\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ and an eighth-order rule inside each, tapered — 480
wavenumber nodes in all. These are deliberately small teaching values, not a
production preset.

**The three orders.** At $k=0.2\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega=0$ the $\ell=0$
coefficients come out in the ratios
$$
\frac{\lvert h^{(1)}_0\rvert}{\lvert h^{(0)}_0\rvert}=0.205,
\qquad
\frac{\lvert h^{(\ge2)}_0\rvert}{\lvert h^{(1)}_0\rvert}=0.162,
$$
so each further collision costs roughly a factor of five here, and their sum
matches `dense_finite_rank_reference` to better than $10^{-10}$. That the
$\ge2$ piece is six times smaller than the free piece is exactly why computing
it as a difference would be a mistake: it would be the fifth digit of a
subtraction.

**The ballistic term.** At $r=20$ m the closed form @eq-ballistic gives a
charge of $3.2885\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm m^{-2}$ and a front time of
$90.06$ ns, and the solver's ballistic component matches it exactly — to zero
error, since both evaluate the same expression.

**The spatial inversion.** Rebuilding @eq-multipole by hand with
`spherical_jn`, contracting with $P_\ell(\nu)$ at $\nu=0.35$, and comparing
against the solver's multiply-scattered component at $r=20$ m agrees to better
than $10^{-12}$. This is the check that the normalisation $1/2\pi^2$, the
factor $\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/2}$ and the phase $i^{\ell}$ of @eq-multipole are the
ones the code uses; a missing $i^\ell$ would leave the magnitude nearly right
and the phase wrong.

**The first order against physical time.** `single_spectrum` at $\omega=0$ is,
by definition, the time integral of `single_scattering_rate`. Integrating the
rate numerically from the front to a horizon of $36/\mu_t v$ reproduces the
spectrum to better than $10^{-6}$ — in this run to $2\times10^{-11}$ — and the
spectrum at zero frequency is exactly real. The two routes share no quadrature:
one integrates over excess path length adaptively, the other over time.

**Does the finite-rank first order agree with the full one?** In the isotropic
geometry — isotropic flash, isotropic receiver, where only $\ell=0$ survives
and the comparison isolates the angular rank of the medium from the angular
resolution of the output — it does, and quickly:

| $r$, m | $L=4$ | $L=8$ | $L=16$ | $L=32$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 10 | $0.9940$ | $0.9999$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ |
| 20 | $1.0004$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ |
| 40 | $1.0004$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ |

each entry being the finite-rank multipole first order divided by
`single_spectrum`. By $L=16$ the two agree to better than $10^{-4}$ everywhere
tested. The finite-rank model is not the problem here.

The directed geometry is a different matter, and it is worth seeing the failure
rather than being told about it. At $r=20$ m and $\nu=0.35$ with $L=8$, $J=12$,
the multipole first order comes out about six times the full-HG value, and
raising $L$, $J$ and $k_{\max}$ together does not fix it: the ratio moves
through $0.86$, $2.7$, $-0.85$, $-1.6$, $0.44$ without settling, changing sign
as it goes. That is the signature of expanding a singular function in a
truncated basis, not of a wrong constant. It is the reason
@eq-production-composition replaces the first order rather than computing it
from the angular route, and it is why the substitution is worth its extra code
path.

**The cache.** On its own grid nodes the stored moments reproduce the hand-built
@eq-multipole to better than $10^{-12}$ for both stored orders — the build is
the formula and nothing else. Between nodes, the interpolation is a genuine
approximation and behaves like one:

| radial nodes | spacing in $\log r$ | relative error at 17.3 m |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 16 | 0.166 | $1.7\times10^{-3}$ |
| 32 | 0.080 | $4.7\times10^{-4}$ |
| 64 | 0.039 | $2.3\times10^{-5}$ |

This is an interpolation check and nothing more: it measures the distance
between the spline and @eq-multipole evaluated at the same $L$, $J$ and
wavenumber rule, so it says nothing about how close either is to the true
transport. The error is not yet asymptotic at 16 nodes and approaches
fourth-order behaviour between 32 and 64, as a cubic spline should. Queries at
half the minimum radius and twice the maximum both raise, naming the range.

**The two first-order routes.** `first_order_consistency` compares the stored
finite-$L$ first order against the full-HG quadrature over twelve radii from
$5.5$ to $54$ m. The median relative difference in the first-order charge is
about $10^{-4}$ and the worst is about $5\times10^{-2}$, which is about $1\%$
of the total charge at that radius. The worst case sits at the short-distance
end, where the forward peak dominates and $L=8$ resolves it least well. Its own
documentation is careful about the attribution, and so is this text: the
residual contains the angular truncation, the radial integration and the
interpolation together, and it is not a measurement of $L$ alone.

## Checks {#sec-scattering-orders-checks}

Fourteen checks are recorded as booleans in the stored summary and the script
exits with a failure if any is false.

**The orders.** Their sum against `dense_finite_rank_reference` below
$10^{-10}$.

**The ballistic term** against @eq-ballistic evaluated by hand.

**The inversion.** A hand-built @eq-multipole against the solver's own
component, below $10^{-12}$.

**The first order.** `single_spectrum` at $\omega=0$ against a direct
integration of `single_scattering_rate` over time, below $10^{-6}$; the
spectrum at zero frequency required to be exactly real; and the finite-rank
multipole first order required to agree with the full-HG one to better than
$10^{-3}$ at $L=16$ in the isotropic geometry.

**The cache.** Stored moments against the hand-built formula on grid nodes,
below $10^{-12}$; interpolation error required to fall monotonically as the
grid is refined and to be below $10^{-4}$ on the finest; extrapolation required
to raise both below and above the range.

**The contract.** `MOMENT_ORDERS` equal to `("one_finite_L", "two_or_more")`,
so that the cache demonstrably does not store the ballistic term; and the saved
component names equal to `ballistic`, `one_exact_HG`, `two_or_more_HG_L`, in
that order. A silent reordering of either would corrupt every downstream sum.

**Everything else.** All arrays finite; NumPy against Numba below $10^{-12}$
when the optional dependency is installed, and recorded as absent when it is
not.

None of this validates the transport against an external result. It validates
that the decomposition sums correctly, that the inversion is the transform it
claims to be, that the first order agrees between two independent quadratures,
and that the cache reproduces the formula it was built from.

## Range of validity {#sec-scattering-orders-validity}

- **Point source, point isotropic receiver.** The $m=0$ problem only; a
  directional module is @sec-directional-om.
- **$K^{(0)}$ for a directed flash is a distribution on the forward ray** and
  the solver refuses that geometry; a finite aperture is needed there.
- **The exact first-order replacement is limited to an isotropic acceptance.**
  A single scalar function of $(r,\nu)$ cannot carry the arrival-direction
  distribution that a directional acceptance needs.
- **The multipole first order is usable in the isotropic geometry and not for a
  directed point source.** In the latter it does not converge, for the reason
  given in @sec-scattering-orders-production, and no setting of $L$, $J$ or
  $k_{\max}$ repairs it.
- **The spatial inversion is a numerical approximation** even though the
  angular tail of @sec-angular-system is exact: $k_{\max}$, the panel width,
  the quadrature order and the taper all enter.
- **$J$ must resolve the angular structure** of the geometry at hand. No rule
  for choosing it is asserted here.
- **The cache is interpolation, not extrapolation**, and is valid only inside
  its radius range and only for the medium, $L$, $J$ and wavenumber rule it was
  built with. Nothing in the stored table records the geometry it will be asked
  about, and nothing in it is specific to a module.
- **The ballistic term is not in the cache**, so any route that reads only the
  cache must add it separately.
- **Time is still a frequency axis.** Nothing here returns a time bin; that is
  @sec-time-and-bins.

## Exercises {#sec-scattering-orders-exercises}

1. Derive @eq-order-two-plus from the resolvent identity and show that
   @eq-order-zero, @eq-order-one and @eq-order-two-plus sum to $h$ exactly. Then expand the full
   resolvent and identify the term with exactly three collisions.
2. Estimate, from the ratios measured in @sec-scattering-orders-example, how
   many significant digits would be lost by computing $h^{(\ge2)}$ as
   $h-h^{(0)}-h^{(1)}$ in double precision at that wavenumber. Repeat for a
   medium ten times less scattering.
3. Derive @eq-ballistic for an isotropic flash from the survival probability
   and the inverse-square law, and confirm the phase by transforming a delta at
   $t=r/v$ with @eq-transform-forward. Why does $\mu_t$ appear rather than
   $\mu_a$?
4. Carry out the angular integral in @sec-scattering-orders-inversion in full,
   including the addition theorem, and verify the constant $1/2\pi^2$ and the
   factor $\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/2}$ of @eq-multipole.
5. Show that for an isotropic flash and an isotropic receiver only $\ell=0$
   survives in @eq-multipole-sum, and evaluate $M_0$ for a non-scattering
   medium to recover @eq-ballistic.
6. Take the four independent quantities named in
   @sec-scattering-orders-question and, for each, give a configuration change
   that alters it while leaving the other three fixed.
7. Explain why @eq-cache-scale carries $\mu_a$ and not $\mu_t$, and predict
   what would happen to the interpolation error if $\mu_t$ were used instead.
8. Explain why `radial_phase="flight"` helps more at large $\omega$ than at
   small, and estimate the radial spacing at which interpolating through
   $e^{i\omega r/v}$ directly would start to fail.
9. State why the exact first-order replacement cannot be applied to a
   directional acceptance, in terms of what `single_spectrum` returns and what
   the contraction would need.
10. Design a test that would separate the $L$ contribution from the
    interpolation contribution in the `first_order_consistency` residual. Say
    which parameter you would vary and what you would hold fixed.
11. The multipole first order converges in the isotropic geometry and not in
    the directed one. Explain the difference in terms of the singularity at the
    ballistic root, and predict what a finite source aperture would do to the
    wavenumber content and hence to the convergence.
